title: Area II review: Preflight Responsibilities
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area II: preflight action and fuel, airworthiness and documents, required and inoperative equipment, and inspections, ADs and preventive maintenance. Many put two of them into one real trip, the way a reviewing instructor would ask.

questions.q: You take off on a personal night VFR trip at 2000, well after the end of evening civil twilight. With forecast winds it is 1 hour 50 minutes to your first stop, at 8.5 GPH normal cruise. On preflight the landing light doesn't work. The airplane has no MEL, and the equipment list, KOEL and ADs don't require the light. What is true, ignoring taxi and climb fuel?
options: You need at least 19.8 gal, using the day reserve, and the flight can't go at night without a landing light
You need at least 22.0 gal, but a landing light is required for every night flight, so it can't be deferred
You need at least 15.6 gal, because the reserve counts only on the trip home, and the light may be deferred
You need at least 22.0 gal; the light is required at night only for hire, so it may be deferred under 91.213(d)
questions.why: Trip fuel is 1.833 hr x 8.5 GPH = 15.6 gal. At night the reserve is 45 minutes: 0.75 x 8.5 = 6.4 gal, so 15.6 + 6.4 = 22.0 gal [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. Night means after the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. The 19.8 gal answer uses the 30-minute day reserve. 91.205(c) requires an electric landing light at night only if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]], so with no other (d)(2) test requiring it, it may be deactivated, placarded and found not a hazard under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)-(4)]].

questions.q: Day VFR. You plan a fuel stop at airport B, 1 hour 40 minutes away with forecast winds, then 1 hour 30 minutes on to your destination C. Normal cruise burn is 9 GPH. What is the least fuel you may begin the flight with, ignoring taxi and climb?
options: 15.0 gal
19.5 gal
21.8 gal
33.0 gal
questions.why: 91.151(a) counts the reserve from the first point of intended landing, which is B [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]. 1.667 hr x 9 GPH = 15.0 gal, plus the day reserve of 0.5 hr x 9 = 4.5 gal, gives 19.5 gal [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. 33.0 gal is (3.167 hr x 9) + 4.5, which plans the whole trip as if you would not stop. 21.8 gal uses the 45-minute night reserve. You still need the same check again before the leg from B to C, and your own margin on top [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

questions.q: IFR to an airport with an RNAV approach. ETA is 1500. The TAF shows 3,000 ft broken and 6 SM until 1530, then 1,800 ft broken and 4 SM. It is 1 hour 50 minutes to the destination, 35 minutes from there to the alternate, at 10.5 GPH. What is the minimum fuel under 91.167?
options: 27.1 gal
33.3 gal
25.4 gal
30.6 gal
questions.why: The alternate leg can be left out only if the forecast shows at least a 2,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]]. Here the ceiling drops to 1,800 ft at 1530, inside that window, so the alternate fuel counts. (110 + 35 + 45 min) = 190 min = 3.167 hr x 10.5 GPH = 33.3 gal [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]]. 27.1 gal leaves out the alternate because the ETA weather looks good, and 25.4 gal forgets the 45 minutes after the alternate.

questions.q: Low on fuel after a long hold, you declare an emergency. To land sooner you turn toward the airport and descend without waiting for a clearance. You land safely. What do the rules require of you afterward?
options: A written report to the FAA within 10 days, because a 'minimum fuel' call should have come first
Nothing: an emergency excuses the deviation, so no report of any kind is needed
A written report to the ATC facility manager within 48 hours, in every case
Tell ATC about the deviation as soon as possible; a written report only if the FAA asks
questions.why: In an emergency the PIC may deviate from any part 91 rule as far as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. A PIC who deviates from an ATC clearance in an emergency must tell ATC about it as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]. A written report is sent only on the Administrator's request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]]. The 48-hour report is for a pilot given priority without deviating from a rule, and only if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]. 'Minimum fuel' is an advisory, not a required first step: if you need priority, declare the emergency [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

questions.q: Your 1965 airplane was not type certificated with a flight manual and flew long before March 1, 1979. Its limitations are in placards, markings and an owner's manual. You plan a trip to a short grass strip. What takeoff and landing information does 91.103(b) require you to know?
options: None: 91.103(b) applies only to aircraft required to have an approved flight manual, so book data is optional here
Only the runway lengths, because without an approved manual there is no performance data you must know
Runway lengths, plus other reliable performance information for the expected elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature
Only the performance information needed when the flight is not in the vicinity of an airport, plus runway lengths
questions.why: 21.5 requires an approved flight manual only for airplanes with no flight time before March 1, 1979 [[60:34|14 CFR 21.5(a)]], so this airplane is not one that must carry approved distance data. For any flight, 91.103(b) still asks for runway lengths, and for aircraft like this one, other reliable performance information for the expected elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. The 'not in the vicinity of an airport' wording belongs to paragraph (a), not (b).

questions.q: You will land on a dry grass strip at sea level, 59 °F, no wind, at 1,600 lb. The PHAK sample landing table gives 445 ft ground roll and 1,075 ft total to clear a 50 ft obstacle on a hard surface. Its grass note says: increase both distances by 20% of the total-to-clear-50-ft figure. What numbers do you plan with?
options: 534 ft ground roll and 1,290 ft total
660 ft ground roll and 1,290 ft total
445 ft ground roll and 1,290 ft total
660 ft ground roll and 1,505 ft total
questions.why: 91.103(b) asks for runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance information on every flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. Note 3 of the table adds 20% of the total-to-clear-50-ft figure to both numbers [[1:283|PHAK Figure 11-32]]: 0.20 x 1,075 = 215 ft, so 445 + 215 = 660 ft and 1,075 + 215 = 1,290 ft. 534 ft takes 20% of the ground roll instead, and 1,505 ft adds the 215 ft twice. Then compare 1,290 ft with the runway length, and remember book numbers come from a brand new airplane flown by a test pilot [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

questions.q: A club airplane had its annual two months ago. Its maintenance manual has an airworthiness limitations section, and the life-limited parts record shows one part passed its mandatory replacement time 6 hours of time in service ago. The club says the annual makes it legal until next year. What is true?
options: The club is right: the annual covers every inspection and replacement time
It may fly 4 more hours under the 10-hour allowance
It may not be operated until that part is replaced as the airworthiness limitations section requires
It may fly, but only without passengers
questions.why: No person may operate an aircraft whose maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness have an airworthiness limitations section unless its mandatory replacement times and inspection intervals have been met [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(c)]]. The status of life-limited parts is one of the records the owner must keep, so check it, not just the annual [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(ii)]]. A current annual doesn't override 91.403(c), and the 10-hour allowance is only for reaching a 100-hour inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. As PIC you may not fly it unless it is airworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

questions.q: Your friend owned his airplane alone and died six weeks ago. The registration certificate in the airplane shows an expiration date in 2031, and the annual is current. His family asks you to fly it to a buyer's airport. What is true?
options: You may fly it, since the registration certificate is good until the 2031 date printed on it and the annual is current
You may fly it until 60 days after his death, which is the time the estate has to return the certificate
You may not fly it: registration ended 30 days after his death, so the airworthiness certificate is not effective
You may fly it with the executor's written permission, since the estate now holds the registration
questions.why: A registration certificate stays effective only until certain events, one of which is 30 days after the death of the holder [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]]. The 60 days is the time the estate has to return the certificate, not extra flying time [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(b)]]. No person may operate the airplane without an effective registration [[60:156|14 CFR 47.3(b)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]], and an airworthiness certificate is effective only as long as the aircraft is registered in the United States [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]].

questions.q: The last annual ran out at the end of last month. This week the IA's new entry says the airplane was inspected in accordance with an annual inspection and a dated list of discrepancies and unairworthy items, including a cracked engine mount, was given to the owner. What does this mean?
options: It is not approved for return to service; it may not fly until the items are repaired and it is approved
The airplane is approved for return to service and may fly for 30 days while the owner orders the parts
The annual is done and the airplane is approved, so it may fly for 12 calendar months from the entry date
The airplane may fly once a private pilot owner signs the list and accepts the unairworthy items
questions.why: That wording is the 43.11 entry for an aircraft not approved for return to service [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]]. 91.409(a) needs an annual and approval for return to service by a person authorized by 43.7 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]], and no one may operate an aircraft after maintenance until it is approved and the record entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. The owner keeps the list of defects until they are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]]. There is no 30-day grace period in these rules.

questions.q: On a rental, the AD status list shows a recurring AD inspection due at 3,250.0 hours. The airplane shows 3,256.0 hours and there is no newer entry. The FBO says, "ADs are the owner's job, not yours. Go fly." What is true?
options: Go: the owner is primarily responsible for AD compliance, so the pilot can't be in violation
Go: the 10-hour allowance covers the extra 6 hours
Don't go: anyone who operates a product that doesn't meet an applicable AD is in violation, each time it is operated
Go, as long as you write the overdue AD in the squawk sheet
questions.why: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for airworthiness, including part 39 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. But anyone who operates a product that does not meet an applicable AD violates 39.7, and does so each time the aircraft is operated [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7]] [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]]. The PIC also decides whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The 10-hour allowance is for the 100-hour inspection only; there is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD itself allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

questions.q: Your annual ran out last month. The FAA issues a special flight permit to fly the airplane to an IA's shop, effective through Friday, and all due ADs are done. Weather keeps you on the ground until Saturday. What is true?
options: You may not fly on that permit Saturday: a special flight permit is effective only for the period it states
You may go Saturday by using the 10-hour allowance
You may go Saturday: like a standard certificate, the permit stays effective while the airplane is registered
You may go Saturday if an A&P without an IA signs a 100-hour inspection first
questions.why: A special flight permit is effective for the period of time specified in the permit [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]]. The open-ended duration, tied to registration and maintenance, is for standard certificates [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]]. An airplane overdue for its annual may fly to the inspection site only on a special flight permit [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], so you need a new one or the inspection done where it sits. The 10-hour allowance is for the 100-hour inspection only [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]], and a 100-hour counts as an annual only if done by a person authorized to do annuals and entered as an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

questions.q: Thirty minutes into a night VFR cross-country, the rotating beacon, your airplane's only anticollision light, fails. What may you do?
options: Finish the whole round trip, because a light that fails in flight needs no action until you land at home
Land at once at the nearest airport and stay there until daylight, because night flight without it is barred
Continue to a stop where it can be repaired or replaced, then fix it or properly defer it before the next takeoff
Defer it under 91.213(d) while airborne by placarding it, and keep flying the planned round trip
questions.why: At night an anticollision light system is required on all U.S.-registered aircraft, and if any light of it fails, the flight may continue to a stop where repairs or replacement can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]]. Deferrals are not for in-flight failures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Before the next takeoff, 91.213 applies again, and an item required by 91.205 for that flight can't be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. A night return with the beacon still dark would not meet 91.205(c).

questions.q: Your flying club has no MEL or LOA for either of two airplanes: a small piston single whose type has an MMEL, and a single-engine turboprop. Each has an inoperative baggage compartment light, and for each one the type certification equipment, equipment list, KOEL and ADs don't require it. For a day VFR flight, which airplane may use 91.213(d)?
options: Both: the light isn't required by the equipment list, KOEL or ADs for either airplane
Only the piston single; the turboprop needs a repair, an MEL with LOA, or a special flight permit
Neither: once an MMEL exists for a type, 91.213(d) is closed and only an MEL with an LOA can be used
Only the turboprop, because the piston single's type has an MMEL and so needs an MEL with an LOA
questions.why: 91.213(d)(1) is about the aircraft before any item test: (i) covers non-turbine-powered airplanes with no MMEL, and (ii) covers non-turbine-powered small airplanes even when an MMEL has been developed [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]]. Turbine-powered airplanes are on neither list, so they can't use 91.213(d) at all [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]]. That is why 'both' is wrong even though the light passes the (d)(2) tests. Without (d), the turboprop can't take off with the item inoperative unless an approved MEL and an LOA in the aircraft provide for it [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]], or under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]. The piston single still needs the item deactivated, placarded and found not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]].

questions.q: Your club's piston single has an approved MEL and an LOA issued to the club. At an away airport you find an inoperative item that the MEL lets you defer, but the MEL binder and the LOA were left at the home office. The club's maintenance officer offers to read you the MEL item by phone. What is true?
options: You can't defer it: the LOA must be in the aircraft and the MEL accessible to you; phone access doesn't count
Since the MEL isn't on board, defer it under 91.213(d) for this flight, treating the airplane as having no MEL
That works if you write down every condition and limitation he reads and keep the notes in the airplane
That works for a day VFR flight only, since a night flight would need the paper MEL on board
questions.why: Taking off under an MEL requires that the aircraft has within it the letter of authorization and that you follow every condition and limitation in the MEL and LOA [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(2)]] [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(5)]]. AC 91-67A says the MEL and LOA must be accessible to the PIC, on paper or digital, and access by telephone, radio or data link is not acceptable [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]]. Switching to 91.213(d) is not an option: once an LOA is issued the MEL is mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], and 91.213(d) excludes operations under paragraph (a) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. Get the documents to the airplane, have the item repaired, or fly under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

questions.q: In your 1978 piston single (no MEL), the stall warning horn doesn't work. A friend says, "It isn't on the 91.205 day VFR list, so placard it and go." What is the correct reasoning?
options: He is right: if it isn't on the 91.205 list, no other rule or document can make a stall warning required
91.205 is one of four tests; the type certification equipment, equipment list or KOEL, and ADs must not require it either
Stall warning devices can always be deferred because the airspeed indicator still works to show your speed margin
It can be deferred only by an A&P who writes the deferral under an MEL for the airplane
questions.why: Under 91.213(d)(2) an item can't be deferred if it is part of the VFR-day type certification equipment, marked required on the equipment list or the KOEL for the flight, required by 91.205 or another part 91 rule, or required by an AD [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. The stall warning device is not on the 91.205(b) list [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]], so the friend has checked only one of the four tests. The PHAK does name the stall warning device as an item that must be repaired before departure, but that example is about an MEL that doesn't list it as deferrable [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], so it doesn't decide a no-MEL airplane by itself. Here the type certification equipment, the equipment list or KOEL, and ADs decide it. If any of them requires it, repair it or fly under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]. With no MEL and LOA, the MEL route is not open [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]].

questions.q: Your non-turbocharged piston single (no MEL) has an inoperative directional gyro. Tonight you plan a personal night VFR flight; tomorrow, an IFR trip. The equipment list marks the DG as standard, the KOEL requires it only for IFR, and no AD applies. What is true?
options: Neither flight may go; a gyro instrument can never be deferred under 91.213(d), even for a night VFR flight
Tonight's flight needs a special flight permit because the DG is standard equipment on the equipment list
Both flights may go if it is placarded, since only the KOEL decides what may be deferred for each flight
Tonight it may be deferred under 91.213(d) once deactivated, placarded and found not a hazard; the IFR trip needs a repair
questions.why: The DG is not on the day or night VFR lists [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]] [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]], and the equipment list, KOEL and ADs don't require it for VFR, so 91.213(d) can be used: remove or deactivate it, placard it "Inoperative," and make the no-hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)-(4)]]. For IFR, 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic direction indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(9)]], and an item the KOEL requires for a kind of operation can't be deferred for it [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]]. If deactivation involves maintenance, part 43 applies [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]].

questions.q: During the runup, your transponder fails its self-test and won't come back. Your VFR route enters Class C airspace about 20 minutes after takeoff. What do the rules allow?
options: Ask the ATC facility with jurisdiction for a deviation, which may be requested at any time
You must ask the ATC facility at least 1 hour before entering the Class C, as for any transponder deviation
Defer it under 91.213(d) by placarding it, and fly the planned route through the Class C as normal
Nothing: an aircraft with an inoperative transponder may not be flown anywhere until it is repaired
questions.why: The transponder is required in Class C airspace [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]], so it is required by another part 91 rule for that flight and can't simply be deferred for it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. ATC may authorize a deviation, requested from the facility with jurisdiction [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(d)]]. To fly with an inoperative transponder to the destination or to a repair shop, the request may be made at any time; the 1-hour rule is for an aircraft not equipped with a transponder [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2)-(3)]].

questions.q: An airplane's annual was done and entered as an annual at 1,640.0 hours. Since then it has flown only private flights. Now, at 1,731.5 hours, its owner, a CFI, wants to start giving paid lessons in it. How many more hours may it fly on paid lessons before it needs another annual or 100-hour?
options: 8.5 hours
None: a separate 100-hour must be done before the first paid lesson
18.5 hours, counting the 10-hour allowance
100 hours, starting from the first paid lesson
questions.why: 91.409(b) applies to flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides, and it is met by an annual or a 100-hour within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. So the annual counts: 1,640.0 + 100 = 1,740.0 hours, and 1,740.0 - 1,731.5 = 8.5 hours left. The extra 10 hours may be used only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, not for more lessons [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

questions.q: Before an IFR flight you tune the departure airport's VOT. The CDI centers with the OBS at 005° and a FROM flag. What is the result?
options: Within limits: 5° is under the 6° limit, which applies to any VOR check including a VOT
Within limits, since the needle is centered and the FROM flag shows a good signal
Out of limits: with a VOT the OBS should read 180° FROM, so 005° is badly off
Out of limits: a VOT should read 0° FROM, and 5° is more than the 4° allowed
questions.why: With a VOT and the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° with FROM, or 180° with TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. 005° FROM is a 5° error. A test signal at the airport of intended departure allows plus or minus 4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. The 6° limit is for airborne checkpoints and airway checks [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]. Don't fly IFR using that VOR until it is fixed or checked within limits by another method [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

questions.q: You fly for a small part 135 charter company. On a day off, the owner asks you to change the spark plugs in one of the company's charter airplanes and sign the logbook, since you hold a commercial certificate. What is true?
options: You may, because a commercial certificate is above the private minimum
You may not under 43.3(g): pilot preventive maintenance is not allowed on an aircraft used under part 135
You may: spark plugs are on the preventive maintenance list
You may, if you sign as a commercial pilot rather than as a private pilot
questions.why: Cleaning or replacing spark plugs is on the appendix A list [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(20)]]. But 43.3(g) lets a pilot do preventive maintenance only on an aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used under part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The certificate level matters for signing off work you are allowed to do [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], not for this limit. A mechanic should do it.

questions.q: Today is October 22, 2026. Tomorrow you fly IFR in your own Cessna. The records show: annual and ELT inspection March 10, 2026; altimeter, static and encoder test and transponder test January 2025; last VOR check September 20, 2026. The static system hasn't been opened. What must you take care of first?
options: The altimeter, static and encoder test, because it was last done in January 2025
The transponder test, because it was last done in January 2025
Nothing: everything is current, so the flight can go as planned
A VOR check, since tomorrow the last one will be 33 days old
questions.why: For IFR using the VOR system, the equipment must have been checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. September 20 to October 23 is 33 days. The altimeter, static and encoder test and the transponder test are good for 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]], so January 2025 tests are still current in October 2026. The annual and ELT inspection are within 12 calendar months [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Log the new check with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

questions.q: An AD requires a recurring inspection of your airplane's fuel selector valve. Years ago a previous owner had a shop repair the valve area. Your new partner says the repair "took the airplane out from under the AD," so the inspections can stop. What is true?
options: The AD still applies; another way to comply needs approval from the manager named in the AD
He is right: a repair or alteration in the area the AD addresses ends the AD for that airplane
The AD now applies only if the airplane is used for hire or flown with passengers aboard
The AD ends once an IA notes the repair in the logbook at the next annual inspection
questions.why: An AD applies to each product it identifies, even if that product was modified, altered or repaired in the area the AD addresses [[60:125|14 CFR 39.15]]. Anyone may propose an alternative method of compliance, but you may use it only if the manager approves it [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]]. Until then, each flight without the recurring inspection is a violation [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]], whether or not the flight is for hire. Keep the AD status record showing when the next inspection is due [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

questions.q: Your annual was signed November 14, 2025. You plan to fly to a friend's airport on November 27, 2026 and return home on December 1. No other inspection is planned. What is true?
options: Both legs are fine: the annual is good for 13 months from the signing date, until December 14, 2026
Neither leg is legal: the annual ran out on November 14, 2026, exactly 12 months after the signing date
Both legs are fine, because you may exceed the annual interval by up to 10 hours of flying to get home
The outbound leg is fine; the return is not, unless you get a new annual or a special flight permit with ADs done
questions.why: Within the preceding 12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. So the annual is good through November 30, 2026: November 27 works, December 1 doesn't. An aircraft overdue for its annual may be flown to where it can be done only on a special flight permit, and all ADs that are due must be done first [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. The 10-hour allowance is for the 100-hour, not the annual [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Plan the alternative now, since 91.103 asks for alternatives if the planned flight can't be completed: an IA at your friend's airport, or an earlier return [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].
